query: We are investigating the atomic-scale thermal behavior of AuCoCuNiPt high-entropy alloy (HENA) nanoparticles synthesized via pulsed laser deposition on a silicon nitride membrane. The prevailing hypothesis is that high entropy and sluggish diffusion stabilize the FCC structure against coalescence and segregation. However, in situ heating experiments reveal a progressive loss of sub-5 nm particles and a widening of the size distribution, alongside a reshaping from elliptical to spherical geometries. Theoretical models based on Gibbs free energy often neglect surface energy terms critical for sub-10 nm systems. It has been observed that the FCC structure in these PLD-grown NPs may be governed by kinetic effects rather than entropy. Propose a mechanism explaining why atomic diffusion is surprisingly active in this quinary system, leading to the segregation of specific elements (like Au and Cu) to the surface and subsequent evaporation. Identify the critical temperature threshold where this mechanism becomes dominant, establish the boundary conditions regarding the initial nanoparticle shape (icosahedral vs. truncated octahedron), and formulate a falsification experiment involving simultaneous in situ STEM and atomistic simulations to test if surface energy gradients alone can explain the observed phase separation without invoking sluggish diffusion.

generation.hypothesis: In sub-5 nm AuCoCuNiPt high-entropy alloy nanoparticles, the 'sluggish diffusion' effect is kinetically overridden by surface energy minimization gradients, driving a non-equilibrium surface segregation of low-surface-energy elements (Au, Cu) and subsequent evaporation, a process that becomes dominant above a critical temperature threshold where surface-to-volume ratio effects exceed the entropic stabilization barrier.
generation.material_initial_state: Sub-5 nm AuCoCuNiPt high-entropy alloy nanoparticles with an elliptical or icosahedral morphology, synthesized via pulsed laser deposition on a silicon nitride membrane, initially exhibiting a kinetically trapped FCC structure.
generation.intervention: In situ heating of the nanoparticles in a vacuum or inert atmosphere within a transmission electron microscope, ramping temperature from ambient to 800 °C at a controlled rate (e.g., 10 °C/min), while simultaneously monitoring morphology and composition.
generation.conditions: Nanoparticle diameter < 10 nm; initial shape anisotropy (elliptical/icosahedral); high surface-to-volume ratio; absence of bulk diffusion constraints due to nanoscale dimensions; temperature range 300–800 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: Surface energy gradients and local lattice distortion at the nanoparticle surface, which lower the activation energy for surface diffusion of specific elements (Au, Cu) relative to the bulk sluggish diffusion predicted by configurational entropy.
generation.mechanism: At temperatures above the critical threshold, the thermodynamic drive to minimize total surface free energy (γ) dominates over the configurational entropy (ΔS_conf) stabilization. This drives rapid surface diffusion of low-surface-energy elements (Au, Cu) to the surface, creating a compositionally depleted core. The resulting surface enrichment lowers the local melting point and increases vapor pressure, leading to selective evaporation of Au/Cu and reshaping of the particle to a sphere (minimum surface area). The 'sluggish diffusion' observed in bulk HEAs is negated by the high surface diffusion coefficient (D_s) and the lack of long-range diffusion paths in sub-5 nm particles.
generation.predicted_outcome: A progressive loss of particle mass (evaporation of Au/Cu), a widening of the size distribution due to differential evaporation rates, and a morphological transition from elliptical/icosahedral to spherical geometry. The FCC structure will persist but with a compositionally segregated shell (Au/Cu-rich) and a core enriched in higher-melting-point elements (Pt, Ni, Co), contradicting the hypothesis of uniform entropy-stabilized solid solutions.
generation.baseline: The prevailing hypothesis that high configurational entropy and sluggish diffusion in quinary HEAs prevent segregation and coalescence, maintaining a uniform FCC structure and particle size distribution up to high temperatures.
generation.boundary: The mechanism is expected to be dominant only for particles < 10 nm where surface energy terms (γ·A) are comparable to or exceed bulk free energy terms (ΔG_bulk). For particles > 50 nm, the sluggish diffusion effect should dominate, and segregation should be minimal or absent.
generation.uncertainty: The exact critical temperature threshold is uncertain due to the lack of direct experimental data on surface diffusion coefficients in sub-5 nm quinary HEAs. The specific role of the initial shape (icosahedral vs. truncated octahedron) in modulating the onset temperature of segregation is also uncertain, as is the precise contribution of kinetic trapping from the PLD process versus thermodynamic driving forces.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform simultaneous in situ STEM imaging and atomistic molecular dynamics (MD) simulations on AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles of varying initial shapes (icosahedral vs. truncated octahedron) and sizes (3 nm, 5 nm, 10 nm). The simulations will explicitly calculate surface energy gradients and diffusion barriers without invoking configurational entropy as a stabilizing factor, while the STEM will track real-time shape evolution and elemental redistribution.
measurements: Real-time particle shape factor (sphericity index) vs. temperature
Elemental composition profiles (Au/Cu vs. Pt/Ni/Co) at the surface vs. core via EELS/EDS
Particle size distribution evolution (number density vs. diameter)
Diffusion coefficients of individual elements derived from MD trajectories
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if: (1) No significant surface segregation of Au/Cu is observed in particles < 5 nm up to 800 °C, or (2) The particle shape remains elliptical/icosahedral without transitioning to spherical, or (3) The MD simulations show that surface energy gradients are insufficient to overcome the activation energy barrier for diffusion without the 'sluggish' effect, and the experimental data matches the simulation predictions of uniform diffusion.
